promptText: What is the core difference between internationalization (i18n) and localization (l10n)?
options: i18n is the engineering work of building an app to support any locale without code changes; l10n is the content work of adapting the app for one specific locale
i18n and l10n are interchangeable terms describing the exact same process
l10n must always happen before i18n in a project's development timeline
i18n refers only to translating visible text, while l10n refers only to currency formatting
explanation: i18n is a one-time engineering investment that makes the app locale-agnostic; l10n is the recurring content operation of actually adapting it per market — you can't localize what wasn't internationalized first.

promptText: Why is using the full English sentence as a translation key (e.g. "Proceed to checkout": "Proceed to checkout") considered risky?
options: Editing the English source text changes the key itself, silently orphaning every other locale's translation that was mapped to the old key
Full-sentence keys are rejected outright by every JSON parser
Using a full sentence as a key makes the translation bundle an order of magnitude larger than id-based keys
Translators are structurally unable to read or work with full sentences, only short identifiers
explanation: Because the key and the English text are the same string, a copy edit to the English source silently breaks the key-to-translation mapping for every other locale with no error thrown — namespaced id-based keys avoid this.

promptText: Why is const label = count === 1 ? "item" : "items" considered a bug in an internationalized application?
options: It hardcodes English's two-category plural assumption, while many languages (Arabic, Polish, Russian) use three to six plural categories with entirely different rules
JavaScript's ternary operator does not support Unicode strings of any kind
The count variable must always be typed as a string, not a number, for pluralization logic to run
This exact line of code throws a runtime error whenever the active locale is not English
explanation: English happens to have only two plural forms, but CLDR defines up to six categories (zero/one/two/few/many/other) used differently across languages — the branching must be delegated to Intl.PluralRules or a library, never a hardcoded ternary.

promptText: What is wrong with formatting currency using "$" + price.toFixed(2)?
options: It hardcodes a symbol, position, and decimal precision that don't hold across locales/currencies — for example the symbol trails the number in some locales, and JPY has no decimal places
toFixed(2) throws a runtime error for any number greater than 1000
String concatenation is measurably slower than Intl.NumberFormat but is otherwise functionally equivalent
The "$" character cannot appear inside a JavaScript template literal
explanation: Currency formatting varies structurally by locale — symbol placement, spacing, and decimal precision all differ — which is why you pass a currency code into Intl.NumberFormat and let it own presentation instead of hand-splicing a symbol.

promptText: What is the advantage of margin-inline-start over margin-left when supporting right-to-left languages?
options: margin-inline-start automatically resolves to the correct physical side (left in LTR, right in RTL) without needing a duplicate [dir="rtl"] override block
margin-inline-start is only recognized by browsers when the active locale is specifically Arabic
margin-left already works correctly for RTL layouts without any code changes needed
Logical properties like margin-inline-start apply only to inline elements such as <span>, never to block-level containers
explanation: CSS logical properties flip automatically based on the current text direction, replacing the legacy pattern of writing physical-direction CSS and then duplicating every rule under a [dir="rtl"] override.

promptText: What does setting <html lang="ar"> actually do for accessibility?
options: It tells assistive technology which pronunciation rules and speech synthesis voice to use, so a screen reader doesn't try to read Arabic text with the wrong phonetics
It only changes the visual font family used to render the page's text
It has no effect on assistive technology unless dir="rtl" is also present on the same element
It functions purely as an SEO signal with no accessibility impact whatsoever
explanation: Screen readers key their pronunciation entirely off the lang attribute at both the document and inline-phrase level — without it, assistive technology defaults to the wrong pronunciation engine for the text's actual language.

promptText: What is the key architectural difference between react-i18next and next-intl?
options: next-intl supports React Server Components, letting fully static translated text ship with zero client-side i18n JavaScript, while react-i18next's client-only model cannot do this
react-i18next only works with class components while next-intl only works with function components
next-intl has no support for pluralization while react-i18next does
The two libraries are functionally identical wrappers around the exact same underlying package
explanation: next-intl was designed after React Server Components existed, so it can render fully translated static markup on the server with no client-side i18n runtime, a capability react-i18next's pre-RSC, client-only model doesn't have.

promptText: A user manually selects "Français" from a language switcher, but on their next visit the app resets to English. What is the most likely bug?
options: The app's Accept-Language/navigator.language auto-detection re-runs on every load without checking for a persisted explicit choice first, silently overriding the manual selection
French does not have a supported ICU plural category, so the app falls back to English by design
Language switchers only affect the current page load and cannot be persisted across sessions by any technical means
Browsers ignore any locale selection that doesn't match the operating system's own default language
explanation: The correct precedence is that an explicit user choice must always outrank automatic detection on every subsequent visit — persisting it in a cookie or localStorage and checking it first before running auto-detection fixes this class of bug.

promptText: Why is splitting translation bundles by both locale and namespace more effective than splitting by locale alone?
options: Splitting only by locale would still ship a homepage visitor the checkout flow's strings; splitting by namespace too means users only download the language and screen-specific strings they actually need
Namespace splitting is required because a single JSON file cannot legally exceed a fixed byte size
Splitting by locale alone is actually more network-efficient, and namespace splitting only adds unnecessary overhead
Browsers cache per-locale files but never cache per-namespace files, making namespace splitting pointless
explanation: Two axes compound: don't ship strings for a language the user doesn't read, and don't ship strings for a feature/route they haven't visited — a large app's checkout or admin copy shouldn't load for someone browsing the homepage.

promptText: A candidate says "just set the i18n key in next.config.js" for locale routing in a Next.js App Router project. Why is this outdated?
options: The built-in i18n config in next.config.js only ever worked with the older Pages Router; the App Router requires implementing locale routing yourself via middleware plus a [locale] dynamic segment
next.config.js no longer exists in any current version of Next.js
i18n routing support was removed from Next.js entirely and now requires a dedicated third-party CDN
The i18n key in next.config.js behaves identically whether the project uses the App Router or the Pages Router
explanation: The App Router dropped the old built-in i18n config key entirely; the modern pattern is a root middleware.ts that redirects to a locale-prefixed path, paired with an app/[locale]/layout.tsx that provides the right messages.

promptText: What is the correct production behavior when a translation key is missing in a specific regional locale like fr-CA?
options: Resolve through a fallback chain (fr-CA to fr to en) so the user sees real text in a related language, rather than a blank space or the raw key string
The application should crash with a thrown error to force immediate translator attention
The raw key like "checkout.submitButton" should always be displayed to production users so they can self-report the gap
Missing keys should silently render as an empty string with no fallback logic configured at all
explanation: A configured fallback chain resolves a missing regional string one step up (to the base language, then a default) so production users always see real text — leaking a raw key or showing a blank is a visible, embarrassing failure mode.

promptText: Why does t("hello") + " " + userName + t("exclamation") break for many languages even though it reads fine in English?
options: It bakes English word order and spacing into the assembled sentence, but many languages need the name in a different position or need surrounding words to change form based on grammatical agreement
String concatenation is technically impossible for non-Latin character encodings in JavaScript
The + operator in JavaScript does not support Unicode strings
This concatenation pattern only fails specifically for right-to-left languages and works for every left-to-right language
explanation: A translatable unit must be a whole sentence with named placeholders so word order and grammatical agreement live inside the translation, per locale — concatenating fragments assembled in application code hardcodes English's shape.

promptText: A team wants to catch hardcoded/untranslated strings and layout overflow bugs before a single real translation has been delivered by translators. What technique accomplishes this, and how does it work?
options: Pseudo-localization — running the UI through a synthetic locale that expands, accents, and brackets every real translation string, making any untranslated hardcoded string stand out immediately against the transformed ones
Waiting for the first real translated locale to ship, then treating any visual bugs discovered at that point as the project's baseline
Running the test suite in headless Chrome with a randomly generated locale header attached to every CI run
Disabling all CSS during testing so that text overflow becomes structurally impossible to observe
explanation: Pseudo-localization transforms genuinely externalized strings (making them longer, accented, and bracketed) while leaving hardcoded strings untouched and visually obvious — catching both overflow and missed externalization long before real translators are involved.

promptText: Why is I agree to the Terms the correct way to handle a translated string containing a link, instead of building an HTML string and rendering it with dangerouslySetInnerHTML?
options: <Trans> keeps the actual <a> element and href under the developer's control in JSX, while the translation only contains numbered placeholder tags the translator can reorder for correct word order — avoiding both broken markup and an XSS surface from translator-controlled HTML
<Trans> is purely a bundle-size optimization and carries no security implications of its own
dangerouslySetInnerHTML is actually the officially recommended approach whenever a translated string contains a link
<Trans> automatically translates the href URL itself into the target locale's own domain
explanation: Passing translator-controlled content into dangerouslySetInnerHTML hands XSS surface to anyone with translation-management-system write access; <Trans> lets translators reorder slotted markup without ever touching the real tag or href.

promptText: A team switches from locale subpaths (example.com/fr/about) to separate ccTLD domains (example.fr/about), expecting search engines to automatically infer the language mapping between the pages. What step is still required regardless of routing strategy?
options: <link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="..."> tags must still be added on every page — search engines don't infer locale-to-URL mapping from the routing strategy alone
No additional step is needed, since ccTLD domains automatically communicate language to all search engines by design
hreflang tags are only required when using locale subpaths and become unnecessary once separate domains are used
Switching to separate ccTLD domains automatically merges search-ranking authority across every locale variant
explanation: Whichever routing strategy is chosen — subpath, subdomain, or separate domain — hreflang annotations are what actually tell search engines which URL serves which locale; the routing scheme alone doesn't provide that signal for free.
